identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: The Sri Krishna Matha in Udupi was founded in the 13th century by the Vaishnavite philosopher Madhvacharya, propagator of the Dvaita school of Vedanta. Krishna is worshipped here as Balakrishna, and devotees do not view the sanctum idol directly but through a carved window known as the Kanakana Kindi. The temple and matha are administered jointly by the eight Ashta Mathas founded by Madhvacharya, which take turns managing worship and administration under the biennial Paryaya system.

governance.managingAuthority: The eight Ashta Mathas of Udupi, administering the temple in rotation under the Paryaya system

narrative.summaryIntro:
The Sri Krishna Matha in Udupi, Karnataka, is a Vaishnavite temple and monastery founded in the 13th century by Madhvacharya, propounder of the Dvaita school of Vedanta philosophy. Krishna is worshipped here in the form of Balakrishna, and the temple is administered jointly by eight monasteries, the Ashta Mathas, that Madhvacharya established with his direct disciples as their founding heads.

A distinctive feature of worship at the matha is that devotees do not see the sanctum idol face to face; darshan is taken through a carved window, the Kanakana Kindi, on the temple's outer wall. Administration and the conduct of daily worship rotate between the eight mathas under the Paryaya system, with each matha's pontiff taking charge for a two-year term.
narrative.documentedHistory:
The matha's own tradition holds that Madhvacharya, while at the port of Malpe, recovered a Krishna idol from a stranded ship, embedded in a large ball of gopichandana clay, and installed it at Udupi; this account is a devotional tradition rather than an independently documented event. The temple's Kerala-influenced architecture and its cluster of shrines developed around this founding.

A further tradition associated with the temple concerns the poet-saint Kanakadasa, a non-Brahmin devotee who, according to the story, was barred from entering the temple; when he stood outside praying, a crack said to have opened in the rear wall let him view the idol, and the temple's chief priest at the time, Vadiraja Tirtha, is said to have had the opening enlarged into a permanent window rather than sealed. This window, the Kanakana Kindi, together with an inner silver-plated window called the Navagraha Kindi, remains the means by which devotees today take darshan of the deity; the legend explaining its origin is recorded as tradition, not verified history.

Administration of the matha and its daily worship is shared among the eight Ashta Mathas — Palimaru, Adamaru, Krishnapura, Puttige, Shirur, Sodhe, Kaniyooru and Pejavara — grouped in four pairs, under the Paryaya system by which each matha's swami takes charge of the temple for a two-year term in strict rotation. Wikipedia notes the Paryaya tradition had completed 500 years as of 2021. The matha lost extensive landholdings following Karnataka's Land Reforms Act of 1975, and its Pauli (outer corridor) was renovated with a Brahmakalashotsava ceremony held on 18 May 2017.

shrines.locationDescription: The main sanctum housing the Krishna idol. Devotees do not view the idol directly; darshan is taken through the outer Kanakana Kindi window and the inner, silver-plated Navagraha Kindi window, which has nine holes.

A window on the temple's rear wall through which devotees take darshan of Krishna. Temple tradition attributes its origin to the saint Kanakadasa, who, barred from the temple as a non-Brahmin, is said to have received darshan through a crack in the wall that the then chief priest, Vadiraja Tirtha, had enlarged into a permanent window; this account is recorded as tradition, not verified history.
A mantapa containing an image of the saint Kanakadasa, within the temple precincts.

poojas.description: The temple's Wikipedia article states that 18 separate poojas are performed daily; individual names and exact timings for each were not available in the sources consulted.

festivals.gregorianRuleOrDate: Every two years, on even-numbered years, around Makara Sankranti (mid-January)
festivals.significance: Marks the handover of temple administration and daily worship from one Ashta Matha to the next in the fixed order of rotation; the tradition is reported to have completed 500 years as of 2021.
festivals.crowdNote: Draws large numbers of pilgrims and dignitaries.

festivals.significance: Celebrates the birth of Krishna, the temple's presiding deity.
